title: Reproducible development, APIs and delivery
summary: One reviewed commit from a laptop to production: five delivery states with their own evidence, a package with tests, a bundle with dev, test and prod targets, three clients of one API, and identities that keep every credential out of code.
outcomes: Place a change in one of five delivery states (local source, validation, reviewed artifact, deployment, execution) and name the evidence that proves it.
Lay a project out as a tested package plus a bundle whose targets carry only environment differences, and predict what dev, test and prod resolve to.
Classify a check as local syntax, local structure, authenticated validation, deployment or execution, and read what validate, plan, deploy and run each prove.
Choose the CLI, the SDK or a raw REST call for a task, authenticate people and pipelines as themselves, and write a promotion checklist ticked only by evidence.
startingAssumptions: The platform module separates workspace, catalog, compute and storage, and the identity module has introduced users, groups and service principals.
Python functions with inputs and outputs, and enough YAML to read nested keys and lists.
editorialRationale: Delivery teaching fails when it becomes a tool tour, so the module opens with five delivery states and their evidence and returns to them at every step: branches and pull requests, the package and its unit tests, pins, per-target configuration, then the bundle's validate, plan, deploy and run as separate states, three clients of one HTTP API, the authentication boundary between people and pipelines, and CI/CD and promotion as gates. Its lab runs only the local state and prints a table saying so, which is the honesty the module asks for.

claims.description: Databricks Asset Bundles were renamed Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs) in Databricks CLI v0.295.0 (18 March 2026) as a non-breaking change: no code or configuration changes are needed, the configuration file is still databricks.yml and the commands are still databricks bundle.
claims.context: Product name changed; command and key spellings did not.

claims.description: The bundle command group includes init, validate, plan, deploy, run, summary, destroy, generate and deployment bind; its help shows the workflow init, deploy --target dev, run, deploy --target prod.

databricks bundle validate checks a target's configuration for errors, warnings and recommendations before deploy, fails on warnings with --strict, and runs an initialize phase that connects to the workspace and reads the current user from the API.
claims.context: CLI v1.17.0; validation needs an authenticated identity.

claims.description: bundle validate reports a reference to an undeclared variable as the error 'reference does not exist: ${var.name}', suggests close names, and prints the bundle name, target, workspace user and path in its summary.
claims.context: Output recorded in the CLI's own acceptance tests, with placeholders.

claims.description: A configuration key the bundle schema does not define is reported as the warning 'unknown field: <name>', and the workspace section deliberately has no token, password or client-secret field: those must come from environment variables.

A target in mode: development prefixes resource names with '[dev <short name>] ', tags them dev, pauses schedules and triggers, limits jobs to 4 concurrent runs, marks pipelines as development and disables the deployment lock unless it is enabled.
claims.context: CLI v1.17.0 presets for development mode.

claims.description: mode accepts only development or production; a production target must set workspace.root_path so only one copy is deployed, an error that becomes a recommendation when every job sets run_as or a service principal deploys, recognized by a UUID user name; development targets keep workspace paths user-specific and may not unpause triggers by preset.

A bundle variable's value comes from --var, then BUNDLE_VAR_<name>, then .databricks/bundle/<target>/variable-overrides.json, then the target's value, then the variable's default; a variable with none of these is an error.

Targets override workspace, variables, resources, run_as, presets, permissions, mode and git settings; a target may not assign a variable the root does not declare, and when several targets exist exactly one may be marked default.
claims.context: CLI v1.17.0 target merging and selection.

claims.description: An include entry without wildcards that matches no file is an error, while a wildcard entry that matches nothing is accepted without any message.
When a target sets git.branch and the checkout is on another branch, bundle plan and deploy stop with 'not on the right Git branch' unless --force is given.

bundle deploy takes a deployment lock, uploads built libraries and synchronized files, records deployment state and applies a plan; deleting or recreating tracked resources such as schemas, pipelines or volumes needs approval, and a console that cannot prompt fails unless --auto-approve is given.

bundle plan shows the actions a deployment would take without changing anything; the direct engine, generally available and the default in CLI v1.17.0, can write the plan as JSON and deploy exactly that file with bundle deploy --plan.
bundle run starts a deployed job through the Jobs run-now call, waits and reports whether the run was canceled, failed, successful, timed out or skipped, unless --no-wait is given.

The CLI's default Python template lays a project out as src/, resources/, tests/ and fixtures/, declares catalog and schema variables in databricks.yml, and defines a default dev target in development mode and a prod target in production mode with an explicit root_path and a CAN_MANAGE permission.
claims.context: Template output recorded in the CLI's acceptance tests.

claims.description: From v1.0.0 the Databricks CLI follows semantic versioning; commands marked Beta or Private Preview and the experimental group may still change in minor releases, and the CLI follows Databricks unified authentication.
Top-level bundle permissions accept CAN_MANAGE, CAN_VIEW and CAN_RUN, and each resource type maps them to its own levels; for a job, CAN_RUN becomes CAN_MANAGE_RUN.
databricks api sends a raw authenticated request for any path, one subcommand per HTTP method, with the body given through --json.

The Databricks SDK for Python (Beta) covers the public Databricks REST API, retries requests that are safe to retry, and its authors encourage pinning the exact SDK version because minor releases may contain documented backward-incompatible changes.
In SDK v0.141.0, WorkspaceClient.jobs.run_now sends POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now with the job ID and optional job parameters and returns a waiter for the run.

The SDK's default authentication uses hard-coded arguments, then Databricks environment variables, then the DEFAULT profile of .databrickscfg, and its README cautions against hard-coding credentials because they can be exposed in version control.
claims.context: SDK v0.141.0; the CLI follows the same unified authentication.

claims.description: Authentication types include pat (host and token), oauth-m2m for a service principal (host, client ID and client secret), external-browser and databricks-cli for a person's OAuth login, and github-oidc workload identity federation, which needs only the host and client ID.

databricks auth login authenticates a person through OAuth in the browser and saves a configuration profile in ~/.databrickscfg that the CLI and SDKs can use; since CLI v1.0.0 interactive OAuth tokens are kept in the operating system's secure store by default.

Databricks Git folders (the Repos API) are a Git client in the workspace for cloning, committing, pushing, pulling and switching branches, intended for version control, collaboration and CI/CD; updating one to a tag leaves a detached HEAD.
A job's run_as names a user, a service principal by application ID, or a group; without it, the job runs as the user who created it.
claims.context: Jobs API as generated in SDK v0.141.0.

claims.description: Databricks secrets hold credentials for notebooks and jobs instead of pasting them in; displayed secret values are redacted, but a user allowed to read a secret can still read it.

databricks bundle schema generates the JSON Schema that describes bundle configuration for validation and autocomplete, and databricks bundle summary lists the resources a bundle deployed with their workspace URLs.
In CLI v1.17.0, bundle deploy on the direct engine reports each resource as soon as it is deployed, and a deploy that fails part way reports the resources it did apply.

Arguments after -- in databricks bundle run are passed to the run, as job parameters when the job uses them; with no resource key, bundle run -- <command> runs a local command with the environment variables that authenticate Databricks tools as the bundle's identity; --no-wait returns without waiting.
databricks bundle destroy removes all Databricks resources created by deploying the bundle to a target, after interactive approval or with --auto-approve.
With the direct deployment engine, databricks bundle plan -o json writes a detailed plan that databricks bundle deploy --plan applies instead of planning again.

A deployment whose plan deletes or recreates tracked resources such as schemas, pipelines or volumes asks for approval, and a non-interactive console fails with advice to use --auto-approve after reviewing the plan.

A run-now request with an idempotency token of at most 64 characters returns the existing run when one with that token exists, so a failed request can be retried until it succeeds and exactly one run is launched.

concepts.definition: Five separate states a change passes through (local source, validation, reviewed artifact, deployment and execution), each proven only by its own evidence.
concepts.example: Green unit tests prove the local state; only a job run ID with a result state proves execution.

concepts.definition: A named line of commits that isolates one change from main until a reviewed merge brings it in.
concepts.example: feature/scrap-rounding holds the rounding fix while main keeps the code prod runs.

concepts.definition: A request to merge a branch that shows its diff to reviewers and runs automated checks before anyone merges it.
concepts.example: The pull request shows the scrap.py change, 14 passing tests and one approving review.

concepts.definition: A workspace folder connected to a remote Git repository, supporting clone, commit, push, pull and branch changes from inside Databricks.
concepts.example: A developer checks out feature/scrap-rounding in a Git folder to explore against dev data.

concepts.definition: Code organized as importable modules of pure functions, called by a small entry point that only handles parameters and input and output.
concepts.example: scrap.py holds the rules; main.py reads the export and calls them.

concepts.definition: An automated check of one function against a small input whose expected output was worked out independently, with no workspace involved.
concepts.example: 1 scrapped of 32 inspected must give 0.0313.

concepts.definition: A check that deployed pieces work together on the real platform, such as a job run in a test workspace whose output is compared with an expectation.
concepts.example: Run scrap_summary in test and compare its summary file with the expected rows.

concepts.definition: The values that legitimately differ between environments, such as catalog, schema and host, kept outside the code and passed in at deployment or run time.
concepts.example: catalog is cinderline_test in test and cinderline_prod in prod.

concepts.definition: Recording the exact version of every dependency and tool so that two builds of one commit resolve to the same software.
concepts.example: pyyaml==6.0.3 rather than pyyaml>=6.

concepts.definition: Databricks' format for declaring a project's resources, artifacts and per-target settings as configuration files that the CLI validates, deploys and runs.
concepts.example: cinderline_scrap declares one job, one wheel artifact and three targets.

concepts.definition: The root configuration file of a bundle, holding bundle, include, variables, artifacts, resources and targets; included files add more resources.
concepts.example: include: resources/*.yml pulls scrap_job.yml into the bundle.

concepts.definition: A named deployment destination in databricks.yml that overrides workspace, variables, mode, identity and permissions for one environment.
concepts.example: --target test deploys to the test workspace as the test service principal.

concepts.definition: A target setting that makes development copies private, prefixed and paused, or makes production targets prove a single fixed deployment location.
concepts.example: In dev the job appears as [dev <short name>] cinderline-scrap-summary.

concepts.definition: A named value declared in databricks.yml, referenced as ${var.name} and given a value per target, by flag, environment variable, overrides file or default.
concepts.example: ${var.catalog} becomes cinderline_prod in prod.

concepts.definition: The CLI command that loads the bundle for a target, authenticates, resolves it and reports errors, warnings and recommendations before any deployment.
concepts.example: databricks bundle validate --strict --target test

concepts.definition: The list of create, update, recreate and delete actions a deployment would take, shown by bundle plan without changing anything.
concepts.example: A plan that recreates a schema deserves a second reviewer before deploy.

concepts.definition: The CLI command that builds artifacts, uploads files and creates or updates the bundle's resources in the target workspace, recording deployment state.
concepts.example: databricks bundle deploy --target test creates or updates the job in test.

concepts.definition: The CLI command that starts a deployed job, pipeline update or app by its resource key and, for a job, waits for its result.
concepts.example: databricks bundle run scrap_summary --target test

concepts.definition: Databricks' command-line tool for people and pipelines, covering workspace APIs, authentication profiles and bundles.
concepts.example: databricks bundle deploy in a CI job.

concepts.definition: A Python library that wraps the Databricks REST API with typed methods, authentication, retries and waiters.
concepts.example: w.jobs.run_now(job_id=...).result() waits for the run.

concepts.definition: The HTTP interface every Databricks client ultimately calls: a method, a versioned path and a JSON body, sent with the calling identity's access token.
concepts.example: POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now with a job ID in the body.

concepts.definition: OAuth sign-in in which a person logs in through a browser and a tool then acts with that person's identity and permissions.
concepts.example: databricks auth login --host https://cinderline-dev.example

concepts.definition: OAuth in which a service principal authenticates with its client ID and client secret, supplied by a secret store, with no person involved.
concepts.example: DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET injected by the CI secret store.

concepts.definition: Authentication in which a pipeline exchanges a token issued by its own platform for a Databricks token, so no Databricks secret is stored.
concepts.example: A GitHub Actions job uses auth type github-oidc with only the host and client ID.

concepts.definition: A Databricks identity for automation rather than a person, identified by an application ID and granted its own permissions.
concepts.example: Application ID 00000000-0000-0000-0000-00000000b001 deploys and runs prod.

concepts.definition: Automation that checks every proposed change (CI) and moves an approved commit through environments (CD) with the same steps each time.
concepts.example: Every pull request runs unit tests; every merge deploys to test.

concepts.definition: Deploying the same reviewed commit, with the next environment's own configuration, after the previous environment's evidence has been accepted.
concepts.example: Commit 7f3c is deployed to test, run and checked, then deployed to prod.

concepts.definition: A plan written to a file by bundle plan -o json and applied unchanged by bundle deploy --plan, so the deployment matches what was reviewed.
concepts.example: plan.json reviewed in the pull request, then deployed by CI.

concepts.definition: The deploy step's pause before deleting or recreating tracked resources, which a non-interactive run can pass only with --auto-approve.
concepts.example: A plan that recreates the quality schema stops the CI deploy.

concepts.definition: A caller-chosen string sent with run-now so that repeating the request returns the existing run instead of starting another.
concepts.example: scrap-2026-09-14 for the export of 14 September.

concepts.definition: The CLI's default place for interactive OAuth tokens since v1.0.0: the operating system's credential store rather than a plaintext cache file.
concepts.example: Keychain on macOS holds the token after databricks auth login.

questions.prompt: The scrap job's pull request shows 14 passing unit tests and a clean local YAML parse. A manager asks whether the job now works in prod. Which answer matches the evidence?

options.text: It proves the local source state only; validation, deployment and a prod run each still need their own evidence.
options.rationale: Right: tests and parsing run on a laptop without a workspace, so they say nothing about the target, the identity or a run.

options.text: Yes: passing unit tests mean the deployment and the run will succeed.
options.rationale: Unit tests exercise functions; a missing permission, root path or volume fails only when the workspace is involved.

options.text: It proves validation for prod, because the YAML parsed.
options.rationale: Parsing is local syntax; bundle validate authenticates and resolves the target, which did not happen.

options.text: It proves execution in test but not yet in prod.
options.rationale: No job ran anywhere; execution evidence is a run ID with a result state.

questions.prompt: An engineer fixes the rounding bug directly on main in the prod workspace's Git folder and pushes; no tests ran. Which safeguard did this skip?

options.text: The pull request, where a reviewer reads the diff and required checks run before main moves.
options.rationale: Right: pushing straight to main bypasses both the reviewer and the automated checks a pull request runs.

options.text: Nothing: a push from a Git folder is equivalent to a reviewed merge.
options.rationale: A Git folder is a Git client; it performs the push but reviews and tests nothing by itself.

options.text: Only the deployment lock of the prod target.
options.rationale: The lock serializes deployments; it has nothing to do with reviewing source changes.

options.text: The unit tests, which Git folders run automatically on every push.
options.rationale: Git folders do not run tests; the CI pipeline runs them on the pull request.

questions.prompt: After the restructuring, which piece of the scrap project can a unit test exercise on a laptop with no Databricks access?

options.text: summarize_scrap in scrap.py, given a list of records.
options.rationale: Right: it is a pure function, records in and rows out, with no Spark session, file or network.

options.text: The job's read of /Volumes/cinderline_prod/quality/exports.
options.rationale: Reading a Unity Catalog volume needs Databricks compute and the job identity's permissions.

options.text: The schedule in resources/scrap_job.yml firing at 06:30 UTC.
options.rationale: A schedule fires only for a deployed job; a laptop can read the YAML but not run the trigger.

options.text: The permissions of the run_as service principal.
options.rationale: Permissions live in the workspace; only an authenticated call can observe them.

questions.prompt: In the transfer export, line L6 inspected 32 parts and scrapped 1. The rule: rate rounded half up to four places; alert when strictly above 0.0400. What does the summary row show?

options.text: 0.0313, no alert.
options.rationale: Right: 1/32 is exactly 0.03125, half up gives 0.0313, and 0.0313 is below the 0.0400 threshold.

options.text: 0.0312, no alert.
options.rationale: That is round-half-even, what Python's round() returns for this tie; the rule says half up.
0.0313 is below 0.0400, and an alert needs a rate strictly above the threshold.

options.text: 0.03125, no alert.
options.rationale: The rule stores four decimal places, so the fifth digit is rounded away.

questions.prompt: A pull request changes alert_threshold to 0.0500 in the prod target only, to reduce noise. What is the main delivery problem?

options.text: Test runs stop predicting prod, because the two targets now apply different business logic.
options.rationale: Right: the threshold decides alerts; with a different value in prod, a passing test run is no longer evidence about prod.

options.text: The CLI refuses any target that overrides a declared variable.
options.rationale: Targets may assign declared variables; the override is legal, which is why a reviewer has to catch it.

options.text: The variable must be renamed separately for each target.
options.rationale: Variables are declared once and assigned per target; renaming would break the ${var} references.

options.text: Nothing: a threshold is configuration just like a catalog name.
options.rationale: A catalog changes where data lives; the threshold changes what the job decides.

questions.prompt: No commit changed, yet Friday's CI run fails while loading YAML and Monday's passed. requirements.txt says pyyaml>=6. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: A newer PyYAML resolved on Friday; pin the tested version with == and upgrade deliberately in its own pull request.
options.rationale: Right: a range lets each build pick a different release, so the build changed while the code did not.

options.text: The workspace changed; rerun databricks bundle validate.
options.rationale: The failure is in CI's local YAML loading, before any workspace is involved.

options.text: The commit is corrupt; revert it.
options.rationale: The same commit passed on Monday, so the difference lies outside the repository.

options.text: A stale cache; rerun until the build is green.
options.rationale: A rerun may pass by luck and leaves the build unreproducible.

questions.prompt: After a refactor, databricks bundle deploy --target test succeeds, but no scrap job exists in test. The root file now says include: [resource/*.yml]. What happened?

options.text: The wildcard matches no file, the CLI accepts an empty wildcard silently, and the bundle deployed without its job.
options.rationale: Right: in CLI v1.17.0 only an include without wildcards that matches nothing is an error.

options.text: The job was deployed to dev instead of test.
options.rationale: The --target flag selected test; the job file was never loaded at all.

options.text: The deploy failed silently; rerun it with --force.
options.rationale: --force overrides the Git branch check; it does not load missing files.

options.text: The job was renamed with a [dev ...] prefix.
options.rationale: The prefix comes from development mode and applies only to resources that exist.

questions.prompt: A prod target sets mode: production but no workspace.root_path, its job has no run_as, and an engineer deploys it from a laptop with a personal login. What does CLI v1.17.0 validation report?

options.text: An error: a production target must set workspace.root_path so that only one copy is deployed.
options.rationale: Right: with neither run_as on every job nor a service principal deploying, the missing root path is an error.

options.text: Nothing, because root_path is optional in every mode.
options.rationale: It is optional in development mode; production validation checks it.

options.text: Only a recommendation, because a person is deploying.
options.rationale: The rule softens to a recommendation when run_as is set on all jobs or a service principal deploys, not for a person.

options.text: It adds a [dev] prefix to keep the copies apart.
options.rationale: Prefixes come from development mode, which this target does not use.

questions.prompt: Which result can only come from databricks bundle validate, and not from a local YAML parse or the lab's local structure rules?

options.text: A summary naming the workspace user the configuration was resolved for.
options.rationale: Right: validate's initialize phase asks the workspace who the current user is; no local check can know that.

options.text: A finding that a target assigns an undeclared variable.
options.rationale: That rule is structural; the lab's local checker reports it without a workspace.

options.text: A duplicate-key error on line 7 of databricks.yml.
options.rationale: A strict local loader finds duplicate keys without any workspace.

options.text: Confirmation that the files are well-formed YAML.
options.rationale: Any YAML parser confirms that locally.

questions.prompt: The CI log shows databricks bundle deploy --target test succeeded. What can the team now claim?

options.text: The job and its files exist in test as configured; the job has not run yet.
options.rationale: Right: deploy creates or updates resources and records state; only bundle run starts a run.

options.text: Today's scrap summary is correct in test.
options.rationale: No run has produced output; correctness needs a run and an output check.

options.text: The prod deployment will succeed too.
options.rationale: Prod has its own root path, identity, permissions and branch rule; its deploy is separate evidence.

options.text: The job ran once as part of the deploy.
options.rationale: Deploy starts no run; a run ID only comes from bundle run or the schedule.

questions.prompt: A Python service must start the scrap job when an export file lands, retry safely on network errors and never start two runs for one file. Which choice fits best?

options.text: The SDK's w.jobs.run_now with an idempotency token derived from the file's export day.
options.rationale: Right: the SDK adds authentication and retries, and the token makes a retried request return the existing run.

options.text: Running databricks bundle deploy every time a file lands.
options.rationale: Deploy changes resources and starts no run; redeploying per file is the wrong operation.

options.text: A raw REST call without an idempotency token, retried in a loop.
options.rationale: If a response is lost, a retry without a token can start a second run.

options.text: Changing the job's schedule to run every minute.
options.rationale: A schedule ignores the file's arrival and starts runs with nothing new to process.

questions.prompt: The CI job that deploys prod must authenticate. Which setup keeps credentials out of code and ties the actions to an automation identity?

options.text: A service principal via OAuth M2M, with client ID and secret injected from the CI secret store, or via workload identity federation.
options.rationale: Right: the principal acts under its own permissions and no credential is written into code or configuration.

options.text: The team lead's personal access token under workspace in databricks.yml.
options.rationale: The bundle's workspace section has no token field, and a person's token ties prod to one employee.

options.text: The team lead running databricks auth login on the CI runner once.
options.rationale: That is a person's browser login; deployments would act as that person.

options.text: A token hard-coded in the SDK call inside main.py.
options.rationale: The SDK README cautions that hard-coded credentials can be exposed through version control.

selfQuestions.prompt: Sketch the scrap project's pipeline in four stages. For each, name the trigger, the command, the identity it runs as and the evidence it leaves.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Pull request: each push to the branch runs unit tests, the local configuration checks and databricks bundle validate --strict --target test as the test service principal, leaving test counts and the validate summary. Merge to main: deploy --target test and run scrap_summary --target test as the same principal, leaving the deploy log, a run ID and the integration-check result. Approval: a second person reviews bundle plan --target prod and records the approval. Prod: deploy the same commit with --target prod as the prod principal, leaving a deploy log with that commit SHA and the first run's ID.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each stage uses the narrowest identity for its environment and records evidence tied to one commit, so no stage relies on an earlier stage's claim. Folding validate into the merge stage is acceptable if it still runs before any deployment.

selfQuestions.prompt: The team wants to promote the scrap change to prod on Friday. The test deploy succeeded, but the test run was skipped because the job was busy. Which two checklist rows would you refuse to tick, and what evidence would unblock each?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Refuse 'test run succeeded': there is a deploy log but no run ID or result state; unblock it with databricks bundle run scrap_summary --target test from the same commit and its run ID with SUCCESS. Refuse 'test output checked': no summary file exists to compare; unblock it by comparing the run's scrap_summary.json with the expected rows for a known export day. A successful deploy is not execution evidence.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Promotion relies on evidence from the state being claimed: a deployment proves resources exist, not that the rules, parameters and permissions work together. Rerunning the same commit is acceptable; testing a different commit is not.

beats.title: A green check proves only its own state
beats.outcome: Place a change in one of five delivery states and name the evidence that proves it.
beats.explanation: A change to Cinderline's scrap job passes through five [[dbxfe-delivery-states-concept|delivery states]]: local source (a commit whose unit tests pass), validation (the bundle checked for a target by an authenticated CLI), reviewed artifact (the approved commit and its plan), deployment (resources created or updated in a workspace) and execution (a job run with a result state). Each leaves different evidence, and none stands in for the next. Notice in the last state that this module's lab ticks only the local state: everything from validation onward is marked not run.

samajh.text: Socho ghar banana hai. Pehle naksha banta hai aur architect use check karta hai: yeh local source hai. Phir municipal office stamp lagata hai: validation. Stamp wala naksha file mein rakha jaata hai: reviewed artifact. Phir asli construction hoti hai: deployment. Aur jab log rehne lagte hain aur paani-bijli sach mein chalte hain, tab execution. Naksha kitna bhi sundar ho, woh ghar mein rehne ka saboot nahi hai.
samajh.mapping: The drawing is the commit and its tests, the municipal stamp is authenticated validation, the filed approved drawing is the reviewed artifact, construction is deployment and people living there is a job run.
samajh.boundary: A software deployment can be repeated or rolled back in minutes and one drawing can be built in three environments; a house cannot.

beats.hint: Ask which evidence each state leaves: a test log, a validate summary, an approval, a deploy log or a run ID.

handbook.markdown:
Keep five states apart when you describe a change, because each fails for different reasons and each leaves different evidence.

| state | what exists | evidence to keep | typical failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| local source | a commit on a branch | commit SHA, unit-test counts | a rule is wrong |
| validation | the bundle resolved for one target | `databricks bundle validate` summary naming the workspace user | unknown field, missing root path, undeclared variable |
| reviewed artifact | approved diff and plan | pull-request approval, the reviewed plan | a reviewer spots a changed threshold |
| deployment | resources in the workspace | deploy log, deployment state | permission denied, destructive plan refused |
| execution | a job run | run ID and result state | the job cannot read its volume |

**How to explain it.** Name the state in every status sentence: "unit tests pass at 7f3c; validated for test; not deployed" is useful, "the pipeline is done" is not a state.

**What to inspect.** For validation, the summary lines Name, Target, Workspace host, User and Path show which identity and target were resolved. For deployment, the deploy log; a deploy on the direct engine that fails part way reports the resources it did apply, so record which changed. For execution, the run's result state and output.

**How to demonstrate honestly.** A local demonstration proves the local state only. This module's lab runs parsing, local structure rules, variable resolution, unit tests and the entry point on a temporary folder, then prints a table marking authentication, validation, plan, deployment, run, integration and promotion as NOT RUN. Showing that table is stronger than implying the rest happened.

beats.recap: Local source, validation, reviewed artifact, deployment, execution: five states, five kinds of evidence.

beats.title: A branch isolates a change until review merges it
beats.outcome: Trace a change from a feature branch through a pull request to main and say what each step proves.
beats.explanation: Work starts on a [[dbxfe-delivery-branch-concept|feature branch]] cut from main, so the running job keeps its code while the fix is built. A [[dbxfe-delivery-pr-concept|pull request]] shows the diff to a reviewer and runs automated checks on it; merging moves main to a commit that was reviewed and tested. Inside the workspace, a [[dbxfe-delivery-gitfolder-concept|Git folder]] is a Git client for the same repository. Notice in the third state that a red check blocks the merge: the branch keeps its commits and main does not move.
beats.hint: Separate what Git records (commits, branches) from what the pull request adds (review, checks).

handbook.markdown:
**Mechanism.** A branch is a movable name for a line of commits. Cinderline's `main` points at the commit prod runs; `feature/scrap-rounding` starts there and collects the fix. A pull request compares the branch head with `main`, shows the diff, runs the required checks and records reviews. Merging moves `main` to a commit that contains the change.

**What a reviewer reads.** Code and configuration together. A one-line change in a target, such as `catalog: cinderline_prod` inside the test target, redirects a job to production data and passes every unit test. Review `databricks.yml` like code: targets, `run_as`, permissions, variables and include patterns.

**Git folders.** Databricks Git folders (the Repos API) are a Git client in the workspace: clone, commit, push, pull, switch branches and compare diffs, for version control, collaboration and CI/CD. The SDK v0.141.0 docstrings note that updating a folder to a tag leaves a detached HEAD, so new commits need a branch first, and that the force-discard option is only for automated folders that mirror a remote branch read-only. People explore in Git folders; deployments come from the pipeline's checkout of a reviewed commit.

**Tying a target to a branch.**

```yaml
targets:
  prod:
    git:
      branch: main
```

With this, `databricks bundle plan` and `deploy` for prod stop with "not on the right Git branch" when the checkout is on another branch, unless `--force` is given, which the CLI warns may push unexpected code.

**What fails.** Direct pushes to `main` skip review and checks; long-lived branches drift and merge painfully; a `--force` in a pipeline script defeats the branch rule.

beats.recap: Branch, pull request with checks and review, merge: main only moves to a reviewed, tested commit.

beats.title: Rules live in a package; the entry point only calls them
beats.outcome: Split a notebook into a testable package and a thin entry point, and say which part runs without a workspace.
beats.explanation: The old scrap notebook mixed four things: reading the export, the rate rules, writing results and a pasted token. A [[dbxfe-delivery-package-concept|modular package]] separates them. scrap.py holds pure functions: records in, rows out, no Spark, files or network. params.py parses the job's arguments. main.py is the thin entry point that reads, calls and writes. Notice in the second state that the rules, the parameters and their tests are marked testable on a laptop, while the entry point's access to a real volume still needs the platform.
beats.hint: For each piece, ask what it needs to run: only its inputs, or a workspace.

handbook.markdown:
**Mechanism.** Divide code by what it needs. Rules need only their inputs, so they belong in pure functions. Parameters need parsing and validation. Input and output need the platform. Keep each in its own module:

```python
# src/cinderline_quality/scrap.py (excerpt)
def scrap_rate(scrapped: int, inspected: int) -> Decimal | None:
    if inspected == 0:
        return None
    return (Decimal(scrapped) / Decimal(inspected)).quantize(
        Decimal("0.0001"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
```

```python
# src/cinderline_quality/main.py (excerpt)
def main(argv=None):
    params = parse_params(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
    folder = Path(export_dir(params))
    records = json.loads((folder / "inspections.json").read_text())
    rows, rejected = summarize_scrap(records, params.alert_threshold)
```

The entry point translates parameters into paths, calls the rules and writes the result. `pyproject.toml` names it as the console script `scrap_summary`, and the job's `python_wheel_task` calls it with `package_name: cinderline_quality` and `entry_point: scrap_summary`.

**Why.** The deployed code is exactly the tested code, another job or a notebook can reuse the rules, and a reviewer reads a short diff instead of a notebook export.

**Notebooks keep a role.** Exploration and one-off analysis stay in notebooks, and a notebook can import the same package so exploration uses the production rules; check the current documentation for how your workspace imports code from a Git folder before relying on it.

**What fails.** Hard-coded paths such as `/Volumes/cinderline_prod/...` that make dev write to prod, credentials in cells, and logic duplicated between a notebook and the job so that fixing one leaves the other wrong. The CLI's default Python template uses the same split: `src/`, `resources/`, `tests/` and `fixtures/`.

beats.recap: Pure rules in a package, a thin entry point for parameters and files, and tests that need no workspace.

beats.title: A unit test pins a rule to numbers worked out by hand
beats.outcome: Predict a rule's output on a tiny dataset and tell a unit test from an integration test.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delivery-unittest-concept|unit test]] feeds one function a few records whose answer you computed independently. Line L6 inspected 32 parts and scrapped 1: exactly 0.03125, which the plant's half-up rule makes 0.0313 while Python's round gives 0.0312. Line L4 inspected nothing, so it has no rate at all. Notice the starter's error row: dividing by zero is caught on a laptop in milliseconds. An [[dbxfe-delivery-integration-concept|integration test]] is a different state: it runs the deployed job in a test workspace and checks the output.
beats.hint: Look for the inputs that separate a right rule from a nearly right one: ties, zeros and boundaries.

handbook.markdown:
**A unit test.** Arrange a few records, act by calling one function, assert against values you computed before running the code:

```python
def test_rate_rounds_half_up_to_four_places(self):
    # 1 / 32 = 0.03125 exactly: half up gives 0.0313 (half even gives 0.0312).
    self.assertEqual(scrap_rate(1, 32), Decimal("0.0313"))
```

Independence matters: an expected value copied from the code's own output proves nothing, so write the derivation beside the test.

**Choose cases that separate right from wrong.** A tie at the fifth decimal separates half up from half even; an idle line separates "no rate" from "zero"; a rate exactly at the threshold separates "above" from "at or above"; a record with more scrapped than inspected tests rejection. In this module's lab the starter package fails exactly these: of 14 tests, 8 passed, 5 failed and 1 raised an error (the division by zero), run locally on synthetic records.

**Integration tests are a later state.** They need the deployed job: deploy to test, `databricks bundle run scrap_summary --target test`, then compare the output with an expected summary for a known input. They catch what unit tests cannot: permissions, paths, parameters as the target renders them, the job's environment. They cost minutes and a workspace, so run them after merge rather than on every keystroke.

**Frameworks.** The lab uses the standard library's `unittest` so it needs nothing installed beyond PyYAML; many projects use pytest. What matters is that CI runs the tests on every pull request and records the counts with the commit SHA.

**What fails.** Tests that read the real volume (integration tests in disguise that fail offline), expected values pasted from the code's own output, and tests that pass because nothing asserts.

beats.recap: Unit tests pin rules to hand-computed numbers on a laptop; integration tests need the deployed job.

beats.title: Configuration carries what differs between environments
beats.outcome: Decide which values belong in per-target configuration and which must stay identical everywhere.
beats.explanation: Catalog, schema and host legitimately differ: dev writes to cinderline_dev, prod to cinderline_prod. Those values are [[dbxfe-delivery-config-concept|environment configuration]], declared once as [[dbxfe-delivery-variable-concept|bundle variables]] and assigned per target; the code only receives parameters. The alert threshold is different in kind: it is a business rule. Notice the third state: if prod overrides it to 0.0500, a passing test run no longer predicts prod's alerts, because the two environments now run different logic.

samajh.text: Darzi ke paas ek hi design ka pattern hota hai. Bachche, papa aur dadaji ke kurte usi pattern se bante hain; sirf naap badalta hai: lambai, chaati, aasteen. Agar darzi kisi ek ke kurte mein chupchaap design hi badal de, toh trial wala kurta baaki kurton ka saboot nahi rehta.
samajh.mapping: The pattern is the code and databricks.yml, the three people are the dev, test and prod targets, the measurements are catalog and schema, and the design is a business rule such as the alert threshold.
samajh.boundary: Targets also change identity, permissions and deployment mode, which a kurta's measurements have no equivalent for; the analogy covers parameters only.

beats.hint: Ask whether a value says where data lives or what the job decides.

handbook.markdown:
**Declare once, assign per target.**

```yaml
variables:
  catalog:
    description: Unity Catalog catalog that holds this target's exports volume.
  schema:
    description: Schema inside that catalog.
  alert_threshold:
    description: Business rule. Scrap rate above which a line is flagged.
    default: "0.0400"
targets:
  test:
    variables:
      catalog: cinderline_test
      schema: quality
```

Reference a variable as `${var.catalog}`: the task receives `--catalog cinderline_test` in test and `--catalog cinderline_prod` in prod, and the code never learns which environment it is in.

**Resolution order** in CLI v1.17.0: the `--var` flag, then the environment variable `BUNDLE_VAR_<name>`, then `.databricks/bundle/<target>/variable-overrides.json`, then the target's value, then the variable's default. With none of these, validation fails with "no value assigned to required variable". A target may assign only variables the root declares, or the CLI reports "variable ... is not defined but is assigned a value", and a reference to an undeclared name fails as "reference does not exist".

**What belongs in configuration:** where data lives (catalog, schema, volume), which workspace (host), who runs and who may see (run_as, permissions) and schedules. **What does not:** business rules, which must match in test and prod for a test run to predict prod; secrets, which come from the environment or a secret scope and never from a variable default.

**What to inspect.** `databricks bundle validate --target prod -o json` prints the resolved configuration with sensitive values redacted (it needs authentication); the lab's `bundlecheck.py --resolve` shows what a laptop can resolve and lists what only the workspace can, such as `${workspace.current_user.short_name}`.

**What fails.** Catalog names hard-coded in code, business rules overridden per target, and values passed with `--var` from one engineer's shell, which leave no record in the repository.

beats.recap: Environment differences are variables assigned per target; business rules stay identical so test evidence transfers.

beats.title: A pin makes tomorrow's build the build you tested
beats.outcome: Diagnose a failure caused by an unpinned dependency and list the tools a delivery pipeline pins.
beats.explanation: An unpinned requirement such as pyyaml>=6 resolves to whatever is newest on the day of the build, so two builds of one commit can differ. [[dbxfe-delivery-pinning-concept|Dependency pinning]] records exact versions: the lab pins pyyaml==6.0.3, the build backend and the build tool. The CLI is pinned too: from v1.0.0 it follows semantic versioning, yet commands marked Beta can still change in minor releases. Notice in the comparison that only the unpinned build changed while the commit stayed the same.
beats.hint: When the code did not change but the result did, look at what the build resolved.

handbook.markdown:
**What to pin.** Everything that can change the build or its behaviour:

| layer | Cinderline example | where |
|---|---|---|
| runtime libraries | none today; any addition as `name==version` | `pyproject.toml` |
| test and lab tools | `pyyaml==6.0.3` | `requirements.txt` |
| build tools | `build==1.6.1`, `setuptools==84.0.0` | `requirements-ci.txt`, `[build-system]` |
| job environment | `environment_version: "5"` and the project wheel | `resources/scrap_job.yml` |
| Databricks CLI | v1.17.0 | the pipeline step that installs it |
| Databricks SDK | `databricks-sdk==0.141.0`, if used | the package's dependencies |

**Why the CLI and SDK too.** The CLI follows semantic versioning from v1.0.0, but commands marked Beta or Private Preview, and the experimental group, may change in any minor release, and a bundle's behaviour is the CLI's behaviour. The SDK's README says the SDK is Beta, asks users to pin the exact version and warns that minor releases may carry documented backward-incompatible changes.

**Upgrade deliberately.** Change a pin in its own pull request, so that its test run isolates the effect. A version range such as `>=6` turns every build into an unannounced upgrade.

**What to inspect.** The resolved environment in CI (the installed versions and `databricks --version`), stored with the build's evidence. If the only difference between a passing and a failing build is the date, suspect an unpinned dependency first.

**Limits.** A pin fixes a version number, not what a package index serves for it; hash-checked installs go further. The job's environment on Databricks has its own base, so verify it against current documentation rather than assuming your pins cover it. In this module's lab the build-tool pins were confirmed to exist on PyPI but were not installed or run.

beats.recap: Pin libraries, build tools, the CLI and the SDK to exact versions; upgrade in a pull request of its own.

beats.title: One databricks.yml declares the whole project
beats.outcome: Read a bundle's root file and name what each top-level key contributes.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-delivery-bundle-concept|Declarative Automation Bundle]], formerly named Databricks Asset Bundles, declares a project as configuration. Its root file, [[dbxfe-delivery-yml-concept|databricks.yml]], names the bundle, includes resource files such as resources/scrap_job.yml, declares variables and artifacts, and lists targets. The rename changed no key or command: it is still databricks.yml and databricks bundle. Notice in the second state that the job is not in the root file at all; it arrives through include, so a mistyped include pattern drops it silently.
beats.hint: Follow the job from the include line to the file that defines it.

handbook.markdown:
**The root file** of Cinderline's bundle (hosts use the reserved `.example` domain):

```yaml
bundle:
  name: cinderline_scrap
include:
  - resources/*.yml
artifacts:
  scrap_wheel:
    type: whl
    path: .
    build: python -m build --wheel
variables: {}   # catalog, schema, alert_threshold (see the configuration beat)
targets: {}     # dev, test, prod (see the targets beat)
```

and the included job, `resources/scrap_job.yml`:

```yaml
resources:
  jobs:
    scrap_summary:
      name: cinderline-scrap-summary
      schedule: {quartz_cron_expression: "0 30 6 * * ?", timezone_id: UTC}
      tasks:
        - task_key: summarize
          environment_key: default
          python_wheel_task:
            package_name: cinderline_quality
            entry_point: scrap_summary
            parameters: [--catalog, "${var.catalog}", --schema, "${var.schema}", --alert-threshold, "${var.alert_threshold}"]
      environments:
        - environment_key: default
          spec: {environment_version: "5", dependencies: [../dist/*.whl]}
```

**The name.** The format was called Databricks Asset Bundles until CLI v0.295.0 (18 March 2026) renamed it Declarative Automation Bundles; the changelog calls the rename non-breaking, and the file, keys and `databricks bundle` commands are unchanged. Search for both names.

**Include.** Only the root file's `include` is processed. An entry without wildcards that matches nothing is an error; a wildcard that matches nothing is not reported, so `resource/*.yml` deploys a bundle with no job. Check the resources you expect with `databricks bundle summary` after a deploy.

**Starting point.** `databricks bundle init default-python` generates `src/`, `resources/`, `tests/`, `fixtures/` and a `databricks.yml` with dev and prod targets; the lab's project follows the same layout.

**The complete key list** for the CLI you pin comes from `databricks bundle schema`, which prints the JSON Schema of bundle configuration; job keys mirror the Jobs API.

beats.recap: databricks.yml names the bundle, includes resource files, declares variables and artifacts, and lists targets.

beats.title: Development and production modes make different promises
beats.outcome: Predict what mode: development and mode: production change for a deployment and which settings production requires.
beats.explanation: Each [[dbxfe-delivery-target-concept|bundle target]] picks a [[dbxfe-delivery-mode-concept|deployment mode]]. Development makes a private copy: names get a '[dev <short name>]' prefix, schedules and triggers pause, and the default root path is the deployer's home folder. Production must prove there is one copy: the CLI requires an explicit workspace.root_path, relaxed to a recommendation only when every job sets run_as or a service principal deploys. Notice in the last state that Cinderline's test target also uses production mode, so test behaves like prod except for its data and identity.
beats.hint: Ask how many copies of the job each mode is designed to produce.
beats.recap: Development gives each person a paused, prefixed copy; production insists on one fixed location.

beats.title: Parsing is local; bundle validate needs an identity
beats.outcome: Classify a check as local syntax, local structure or authenticated validation, and read what validate's output proves.
beats.explanation: Parsing databricks.yml proves only that the text is YAML, and the lab's local rules go one step further by checking structure without a workspace. [[dbxfe-delivery-validate-concept|databricks bundle validate]] is another state: its initialize phase connects to the workspace and asks who the current user is, then resolves variables and paths and applies the full schema and mode rules. Its summary names the workspace host and user before 'Validation OK!', and --strict fails on warnings. Notice in the second state that only validate's arrow crosses into the workspace.
beats.hint: Ask whether the check could possibly know who the current user is.

handbook.markdown:
**Three different checks.**

| check | needs | proves |
|---|---|---|
| YAML parse | a parser | the text is YAML; a plain `yaml.safe_load` even keeps the second of two duplicate keys silently |
| local structure rules | the files | the configuration has the shape the team requires |
| `databricks bundle validate --target test` | an authenticated identity and the workspace | the configuration resolves for that identity and target under the CLI's rules |

**What validate does.** It runs the initialize phase, which fills in defaults and connects to the workspace: it reads the current user from the API, loads Git details, sets the default root path, assigns variables, resolves lookups, applies the target mode, checks required fields and enums, gives permission diagnostics and validates the mode rules. The text summary then names the bundle, target, workspace host, user and path, followed by `Validation OK!` or the errors. `--strict` turns warnings into failures, which matters because an unknown key such as `token` is only a warning: "unknown field: token". `-o json` prints the resolved configuration with sensitive values redacted.

**Reading a failure.** The CLI's own recorded test output for a mistyped variable:

```text
Error: reference does not exist: ${var.hst}

did you mean:
  ${var.host}
```

followed by the summary and `Found 1 error`. The User line shows which identity validated: if a pipeline log shows a person's name there, the pipeline is not authenticating as its service principal.

**What validate does not do.** It uploads nothing, changes no resource and starts no run. A clean validate is evidence for the validation state only.

**Where it runs.** On a laptop with a person's login for dev, and in CI as the target's service principal for test and prod. This module's lab never runs it: without a workspace its table marks validation NOT RUN.

beats.recap: A parse proves YAML, local rules prove structure, and bundle validate proves the configuration resolves for an identity in a workspace.

beats.title: Deploy changes the workspace; run produces the proof
beats.outcome: Order plan, deploy and run, and name the evidence and the typical failure of each.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delivery-plan-concept|bundle plan]] lists what a deployment would create, update, recreate or delete, and changes nothing. [[dbxfe-delivery-deploy-concept|bundle deploy]] takes a lock, uploads the built wheel and the synchronized files, applies the plan and records deployment state; a plan that deletes or recreates a schema, pipeline or volume needs approval first. Only [[dbxfe-delivery-run-concept|bundle run]] executes: it starts the job, waits and reports a result state. Notice that a successful deploy's timeline ends with a job that has never run.
beats.hint: Ask which of the three commands changes the workspace and which one starts the job.

handbook.markdown:
**Plan.** `databricks bundle plan --target test` builds the bundle and lists the actions a deployment would take, without making changes. With the direct engine, generally available and the default in CLI v1.17.0, `databricks bundle plan -o json > plan.json` writes a detailed plan with the reason for each action, and `databricks bundle deploy --plan plan.json` applies exactly that file.

**Deploy.** `databricks bundle deploy --target test` acquires the deployment lock for the target, uploads the libraries built from the artifacts (here the wheel) and the synchronized files under the target's root path, updates deployment state, applies root-path permissions, computes the plan or loads `--plan`, asks approval for destructive actions, applies the plan and releases the lock. Destructive means deleting or recreating tracked resources: schemas, pipelines, volumes, dashboards, database instances, vector search indexes and others. A console that cannot prompt, such as CI, fails with the advice to use `--auto-approve` after reviewing the plan. Other flags: `--force` overrides the Git branch check, `--force-lock` takes a lock someone else holds, and `--fail-on-active-runs` refuses to deploy while jobs are running.

**Run.** `databricks bundle run scrap_summary --target test` calls the Jobs run-now API for the deployed job and waits, reporting a canceled, failed, successful, timed-out or skipped run; `--no-wait` prints the run page URL instead. Parameters can follow `--`, as in `databricks bundle run scrap_summary -- --key value` for a job with job parameters.

**What to inspect.** `databricks bundle summary --target test` lists deployed resources with their workspace URLs, and the run page shows each task's output and error. On the direct engine, a deploy that fails part way reports the resources it did apply.

**What fails.** Deploying with a person's login instead of the service principal, a blanket `--auto-approve` without a reviewed plan, and treating a successful deploy as proof that the job works.

beats.recap: Plan previews, deploy changes the workspace and records state, and run executes and returns the only proof that the job works.

beats.title: The CLI, the SDK and REST reach one API
beats.outcome: Choose the CLI, the SDK or a raw REST call for a task and explain what each adds on top of the HTTP request.
beats.explanation: Every Databricks client ends in the same [[dbxfe-delivery-rest-concept|REST API]]: starting a job run is POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now with a job ID. The [[dbxfe-delivery-sdk-concept|Databricks SDK for Python]] wraps that call as w.jobs.run_now with typed arguments, authentication, retries and a waiter. The [[dbxfe-delivery-cli-concept|Databricks CLI]] wraps the same APIs for people and pipelines and adds profiles and bundles; bundle run itself calls run-now through the Go SDK. Notice in the second state that the workspace receives one identical request whichever client sent it.

samajh.text: Bank mein paise bhejne ke teen raaste hain: branch ke counter pe form bharo, mobile app use karo, ya bank ka seedha payment interface apne software se call karo. Teeno raaste aakhir mein ek hi ledger mein ek hi entry karte hain. Farak bas itna hai ki counter aur app tumhare liye form bharte hain, galti pakadte hain aur zarurat pade toh dobara koshish karte hain; seedhe interface mein yeh sab tumhe khud karna padta hai.
samajh.mapping: The ledger entry is the REST request, the counter is the CLI, the mobile app is the SDK and the direct payment interface is a raw REST call.
samajh.boundary: Unlike a bank channel, the CLI also deploys bundles, which declare many resources rather than send one request, and all three clients act with the permissions of whoever authenticated.

beats.hint: Strip each client down to the HTTP request it sends, then ask what it added on the way.

handbook.markdown:
**One request underneath.** Starting a run is `POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now` with a JSON body holding the job ID and, optionally, job parameters and an idempotency token, sent with an access token for the calling identity.

**The SDK.** The Databricks SDK for Python covers the public REST API:

```python
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

w = WorkspaceClient()  # host and credentials from the environment or a profile
waiter = w.jobs.run_now(job_id=job_id, idempotency_token=f"scrap-{export_day}")
run = waiter.result()  # waits for the run to finish
print(run.state.result_state)
```

It adds typed arguments, the default authentication chain, retries for failures that are safe to retry (HTTP 429 and 503, connection resets, timeouts) and waiters for long-running operations. It is labelled Beta; pin its exact version.

**The CLI.** The same APIs as commands for people and pipelines, plus profiles and bundles. `databricks bundle run` calls run-now through the Go SDK; where no dedicated command exists, `databricks api post /api/2.2/jobs/run-now --json '{"job_id": 123}'` sends a raw request with the CLI's authentication.

**Raw REST.** Any HTTP client and a token: you own authentication, retries, pagination and waiting. Use it from a language without an SDK, or when you must control the exact request.

| task | fits best |
|---|---|
| deploy a bundle from CI | CLI |
| start a run when a file lands, from a Python service | SDK with an idempotency token |
| trigger from a tool that only speaks HTTP | REST |
| explore an endpoint once | `databricks api` |

**What fails.** Retrying run-now without an idempotency token can start two runs if the first response was lost; hard-coding a token into any of the three clients defeats the authentication chain; different SDK versions in different jobs give different behaviour for the same code.

beats.recap: REST is the contract; the SDK adds types, authentication, retries and waiters; the CLI adds commands, profiles and bundles.

beats.title: People log in; pipelines authenticate as service principals
beats.outcome: Pick the authentication for a person, a pipeline and a federated pipeline, and keep every token out of code.
beats.explanation: A person uses [[dbxfe-delivery-u2m-concept|OAuth user-to-machine]]: databricks auth login opens a browser and saves a profile, so tools act with that person's permissions. A pipeline authenticates as a [[dbxfe-delivery-principal-concept|service principal]] through [[dbxfe-delivery-m2m-concept|OAuth machine-to-machine]], with client ID and secret injected by the CI secret store, or through workload identity federation with no stored secret. Code and databricks.yml hold no credential: the bundle's workspace section has no token field. Notice that the leaked token in the last state reaches everyone who can read the repository.

samajh.text: Society mein residents apni chaabi se apna ghar kholte hain: woh U2M hai. Doodhwale ki van ko society office se gate pass milta hai, jo zarurat pade toh cancel bhi ho sakta hai: woh service principal hai. Aur koi apni master chaabi notice board pe tape nahi karta, kyunki notice board sab padhte hain. Git repository wahi notice board hai.
samajh.mapping: Residents' own keys are OAuth user logins, the van's revocable gate pass is a service principal's OAuth credential or federated token, and the notice board is the Git repository where a pasted token would be readable by everyone.
samajh.boundary: OAuth tokens expire and carry scopes, and federation needs no stored pass at all; a physical key has neither property.

beats.hint: For each caller, ask who is acting and where the credential lives while nobody is looking.

handbook.markdown:
**People: OAuth user-to-machine.** `databricks auth login --host https://cinderline-dev.example` opens a browser, completes an OAuth sign-in and saves a profile in `~/.databrickscfg` that the CLI and SDKs can use with `--profile`. From CLI v1.0.0 the interactive token is stored in the operating system's secure store by default (Keychain, Credential Manager or Secret Service). The CLI and the SDK (`auth_type="databricks-cli"` or `"external-browser"`) then act with that person's permissions: right for dev, wrong for prod.

**Pipelines: service principals.** A service principal is an identity for automation, identified by an application ID.

| method | configuration | stored secret |
|---|---|---|
| OAuth M2M (`oauth-m2m`) | `DATABRICKS_HOST`, `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID`, `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET` | yes, in the CI secret store |
| workload identity federation (for example `github-oidc`) | `DATABRICKS_HOST`, `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` | none: the CI platform's own token is exchanged |

Federation also needs account-side configuration that trusts the CI platform's tokens; check the current documentation for your provider before relying on it.

**Who deploys versus who runs.** The pipeline's identity deploys; the job runs as its `run_as` identity, or as its creator when `run_as` is absent. Cinderline uses one service principal per environment for both and grants it CAN_MANAGE in the bundle's permissions.

**No tokens in code.** The SDK's default chain reads hard-coded arguments, then environment variables, then the DEFAULT profile, and its README cautions that hard-coded credentials can be exposed through version control. The bundle's workspace section has no token or secret field at all. Credentials a job needs for an external system belong in a Databricks secret scope; displayed values are redacted, but anyone allowed to read a secret can still read it, so scope permissions matter.

**What fails.** One engineer's personal token in CI, so actions look like that person's and break when they leave; a token pasted in a notebook and committed (revoke and rotate it, since history keeps it); header debugging switched on in a shared log, which prints access tokens.

beats.recap: People log in with OAuth U2M; pipelines use a service principal through M2M or federation; no credential lives in code or configuration.

beats.title: CI checks every change; CD moves only merged commits
beats.outcome: Lay out a pipeline's gates from pull request to prod and say which identity runs each.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delivery-cicd-concept|CI/CD]] turns the delivery states into gates. On every pull request, CI runs the unit tests, the local configuration checks and bundle validate --strict for test. On merge to main, CD deploys test as the test service principal, runs the job and checks its output. Prod follows only after an approval, deploying the same commit. Notice the failing gate in the last state: the pipeline stops there, and nothing downstream runs on hope.
beats.hint: Give every gate a trigger, a command, an identity and a piece of evidence.

handbook.markdown:
**Gates, not scripts.** A pipeline for the scrap project, independent of the CI product:

```text
on pull request (identity: test service principal)
  pip install -r requirements.txt              # pinned tools
  PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -t tests
  local configuration checks                   # parse, structure rules
  databricks bundle validate --strict --target test
on merge to main (identity: test service principal)
  databricks bundle deploy --target test
  databricks bundle run scrap_summary --target test
  integration check of the summary file
on approval (identity: prod service principal)
  databricks bundle plan --target prod         # reviewed by a second person
  databricks bundle deploy --target prod
```

Every step records the commit SHA, the CLI version (`databricks --version`) and the identity it ran as.

**Identities.** One service principal per environment, authenticated through OAuth M2M with secrets from the CI system's store, or through federation. The prod principal's credentials are available only to the approved prod stage.

**Non-interactive deploys.** CI cannot answer the destructive-change prompt, so a deploy whose plan deletes or recreates a schema or pipeline fails unless `--auto-approve` is passed. Pass it only after a reviewed plan; with the direct engine, attach the plan to the pull request (`bundle plan -o json`) and apply that file (`bundle deploy --plan`).

**The branch rule.** `git.branch: main` on the prod target makes the CLI refuse to plan or deploy prod from another branch unless `--force`; keep `--force` out of pipeline scripts.

**Scripts with the bundle's identity.** `databricks bundle run -- <command>` runs a local command with the environment variables Databricks tools use to authenticate as the bundle's identity, which suits an integration check written as a script.

**What fails.** A pipeline that deploys prod on every push, a shared personal token in CI variables, and a red gate rerun until it passes without anyone reading why.

beats.recap: Pull requests get tests and validation; merges deploy and run test; prod gets the same commit after an approval.

beats.title: Promotion moves one commit with evidence at every gate
beats.outcome: Write a promotion checklist that names the evidence for each gate and marks what is still unproven.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-delivery-promotion-concept|Promotion]] deploys the same reviewed commit to the next environment with that environment's own configuration. It is not copying notebooks or re-running a test in prod. Each checklist row names its evidence: the approved pull request, unit-test counts at that commit, the validate summary, the reviewed plan, the test run's ID and output check, then a prod deploy log carrying the same commit SHA. Notice the second state: the lab can tick only the local rows, and it says so.
beats.hint: A gate is ticked by its own evidence, never by a neighbouring gate's.

handbook.markdown:
**Promotion moves a commit.** The unit of promotion is the reviewed commit SHA together with each target's own configuration. Rebuilding the wheel from that commit with pinned tools gives the same software; copying notebook text between workspaces does not, because nothing ties the copy to a review.

**A checklist with evidence** (abridged from the lab's PROMOTION.md):

| gate | evidence |
|---|---|
| pull request approved by someone other than the author | the approval on the diff |
| unit tests pass at the merge commit | CI log with the SHA and the counts |
| local rules and `validate --strict` for test pass | checker output; validate summary naming the test principal |
| deployed and run in test | deploy log with the SHA; run ID with SUCCESS |
| test output checked | summary file compared with the expected rows |
| prod target reviewed | fixed root path, `run_as`, `git.branch: main`, permissions |
| prod plan reviewed, prod deployed | plan approval; deploy log with the same SHA |
| first prod run observed | run ID and result state |

**Rollback.** Redeploy the previous release's commit through the same pipeline. `databricks bundle destroy` removes every resource the bundle deployed to a target; it is not a rollback.

**Explaining status honestly.** Say which gates have evidence: "validated and deployed to test at 7f3c; test run pending; prod not started". In this module's lab only the local gates ran (unit tests, local rules, resolved parameters); every workspace gate is marked NOT RUN, and the checklist says so rather than implying progress.

**What fails.** Ticking a gate from a neighbouring gate's evidence (a successful deploy is not a successful run), promoting a different commit than the one tested, and approving in chat, where the pipeline cannot see it.

beats.recap: Promote one commit, and tick a gate only when its own evidence exists.

extensionCards.prompt: How can CI deploy exactly the plan a reviewer approved, and nothing else?
extensionCards.answer: With the direct engine, write the plan to a file with bundle plan -o json, review that file, then apply it unchanged with bundle deploy --plan.
extensionCards.explanation: A reviewer who approves a pull request has seen the diff, not necessarily the actions a deployment will take. With the direct deployment engine, generally available and the default in CLI v1.17.0, `databricks bundle plan -o json > plan.json` writes a detailed [[dbxfe-delivery-extension-saved-plan-concept|saved deployment plan]] with the reason for each action; attach it to the pull request, and let the pipeline run `databricks bundle deploy --plan plan.json`, which applies that file instead of planning again. The deployment then matches what was reviewed even if the workspace changed in between. The flag is direct-engine only, so a bundle still on the Terraform engine cannot use it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It closes the gap between a reviewed diff and the actions actually taken against the workspace, which is where a surprise delete comes from.

extensionCards.prompt: Why does a deploy that recreates the quality schema fail in CI after a clean validate?
extensionCards.answer: Because deploy asks for approval before deleting or recreating tracked resources, and a non-interactive console cannot answer; only --auto-approve after a reviewed plan passes it.
extensionCards.explanation: Validate resolves configuration; it does not compare it with what is deployed. Deploy computes the plan, and when the plan deletes or recreates a tracked resource, such as a schema, pipeline, volume or dashboard, it pauses for [[dbxfe-delivery-extension-approval-concept|destructive-change approval]]. A CI console cannot prompt, so the deploy fails with advice to use `--auto-approve` after reviewing the plan. The right response is to read the plan, decide whether the recreate is intended (a schema recreate can drop data), and only then rerun with the flag; a blanket `--auto-approve` in every pipeline script removes the one pause that protects data.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It explains a failure that looks like a bug and is actually a safeguard, and it names the one flag that should never be applied blindly.

extensionCards.prompt: How do you retry a lost run-now request without starting a second run?
extensionCards.answer: Send an idempotency token of at most 64 characters; a repeat with the same token returns the existing run instead of creating another.
extensionCards.explanation: A run-now request can succeed on the server while its response is lost on the way back, so a naive retry starts a second run of the same export. The Jobs API's [[dbxfe-delivery-extension-idempotency-concept|idempotency token]] solves this: if a run with the provided token already exists, the request returns that run's ID instead of creating a new one, so a caller can retry until the request succeeds and exactly one run is launched. Derive the token from the unit of work, such as `scrap-2026-09-14` for one export day, and pass it as `idempotency_token` in the SDK's `w.jobs.run_now` or in the raw JSON body.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Retries are the normal case in automation, and without a token the safe-looking retry is the one that double-processes a day.

extensionCards.prompt: Where does databricks auth login keep a person's token since CLI v1.0.0, and what changed?
extensionCards.answer: In the operating system's secure store by default rather than a plaintext cache file; old cached tokens are not migrated, and DATABRICKS_AUTH_STORAGE=plaintext keeps file storage.
extensionCards.explanation: Before v1.0.0 the CLI cached interactive OAuth tokens in `~/.databricks/token-cache.json`. From v1.0.0 the default is [[dbxfe-delivery-extension-token-store-concept|OS secure token storage]]: the Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows or the Secret Service on Linux. Existing cached tokens are not migrated, so each profile logs in again once, and an environment that has no secure store can set `DATABRICKS_AUTH_STORAGE=plaintext` to keep the file. This is a laptop concern: a pipeline never runs `auth login`, and a person's token should never be copied out of the store into CI.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It explains a one-time re-login that looks like breakage after an upgrade and shows where a person's credential actually lives.

recap.title: Five states, one commit
recap.markdown: **Local source, validation, reviewed artifact, deployment and execution each leave their own evidence, and a green earlier state never stands in for a later one.** The package keeps rules testable on a laptop; `databricks.yml` keeps environment differences in targets and business rules identical; validate, plan, deploy and run are four commands for four states; the CLI, the SDK and REST reach one API; people log in with OAuth and pipelines act as service principals with no credential in code; promotion moves one reviewed commit through gates ticked only by evidence. **Transfer challenge:** take a pipeline you know, list its stages, and write beside each the state it proves, the identity it runs as and the evidence it leaves; mark every stage that is claimed without evidence.

appliedTask.title: Add the supplier-returns job to the bundle
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline wants a second job, supplier_returns, in the same bundle: logic the quality team wrote in a notebook, reading a different export from the same volume and writing to the same schema, due in prod next week through the existing pipeline. List the changes to the project and to databricks.yml, which values become variables and which must not, the gates the change passes and the identity of each, and the evidence you would require before ticking each promotion row. Mark what you cannot know from this description.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Move the notebook's rules into the package as pure functions with unit tests whose expected values are worked out by hand, and give the job a second console-script entry point; add resources/supplier_returns_job.yml with a python_wheel_task naming that entry point, its parameters rendered from the existing catalog and schema variables plus a new export_name variable assigned per target. Nothing new becomes a variable for a business rule: any threshold the returns logic uses keeps one default everywhere. The existing targets need no new identity; the two service principals already hold CAN_MANAGE, and dev's development mode will prefix and pause the new job automatically. Gates: pull request runs the enlarged unit-test suite, the local structure rules and validate --strict --target test as the test principal; merge deploys test, runs supplier_returns and compares its summary with an expected file for one known export day; a second person reviews bundle plan --target prod, which should show exactly one job to create and no change to scrap_summary; the prod principal deploys the same commit. Promotion rows: approval on the diff, test counts at the SHA, the validate summary naming the test principal, the reviewed plan, run ID with SUCCESS and the output check, the prod deploy log with the same SHA, then the first scheduled prod run observed. Unknown from the description: the export's schema and volume path, whether the notebook used any credential (which must move to a secret scope), the returns job's schedule, and whether the prod plan will touch anything else.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer reuses every mechanism the module taught on a changed situation: package over notebook, variables for environment differences only, the same gates and identities, and evidence per row rather than a claim of readiness. Keeping the notebook as a notebook_task inside the bundle with a hand-computed integration check is an acceptable alternative if the rules are made importable later.
